title: Friday Reflection: Strategy Begins with Questions
author: Historically Thinking
summary: This Friday Reflection distils a Historically Thinking conversation with Eliot Cohen about his book The Strategist. Cohen defines strategy narrowly, following Clausewitz, as the use of military force to pursue the ends of policy, and defines a strategist as someone who makes and implements strategy, not merely studies it. At the centre are seven questions: what else is going on, who are those guys, what is the objective, what are the means, what is the priority, what is the sequence, and what is the theory of victory. Because war constantly surprises planners, Cohen turns from technique to four virtues: courage, honesty, empathy and curiosity, illustrated by Churchill's shipboard memoranda after Pearl Harbor. The reflection ends by contrasting historical thought, with its attention to contingency and context, with generalising political science, and concludes that in strategy the quality of the question may matter more than the confidence of the answer.
points: Strategy is the link between force and political purpose, so tactical success that fails to secure the political aim is not strategic success.
Cohen's seven questions expose hidden assumptions, and the last, the theory of victory, forces leaders to state the causal story from inputs to outcome.
Detailed plans create a false sense of predictability, so good strategy depends on spotting error and adapting fast.
Courage, honesty, empathy and curiosity matter because no method can remove uncertainty.
History does not give rules but makes leaders more alert to context and more suspicious of easy analogies.
quotes: That is why strategy cannot be reduced to a procedure. It demands choices among competing priorities, adaptations to changing circumstances, and decisions made with inadequate information.
Claims that the United States has never been defeated militarily miss the point: tactical success is not strategically decisive if it fails to secure the desired political result.

A strategist makes and implements it. Strategy is therefore iterative: decisions alter circumstances, circumstances frustrate plans, and leaders must continually reconsider what they are trying to accomplish.

What is the theory of victory? A strategist must explain why particular actions and resources should produce the desired political outcome. Governments frequently debate inputs without articulating the causal story connecting those inputs to success.
These questions constitute a discipline rather than a formula. They cannot eliminate uncertainty, but they can expose assumptions that would otherwise remain hidden.

Plans are necessary, but reality will not conform to them. Surprise may arise from the enemy, unexpected technological effects, institutional weakness, wishful thinking, physical illness, age, exhaustion, or the dispositions of individual leaders. Strategy therefore depends less upon getting everything right beforehand than upon recognizing error and adapting quickly.

Courage enables a leader to decide without certainty. Honesty permits the strategist to admit that assumptions have failed or that conditions are worse than expected. Empathy makes it possible to understand adversaries, allies, and one’s own side from perspectives other than one’s own. Curiosity sustains the search for information that might challenge settled beliefs.

History cannot tell strategists exactly what to do. It is not a guidebook, or set of rules. But it can make them more alert to context, more suspicious of simple analogies, and better able to ask questions. In strategy, as in historical thinking, the quality of the question may matter more than the confidence of the answer.
